description: Elevate your Java skills with streams, concurrency, and architecture patterns used in modern back-end systems.

days.title: Day 30 – Java Data Structures Fundamentals
days.definition: Java Data Structures are collections in the java.util package that provide efficient ways to store, organize, and manipulate data, going beyond basic arrays with enhanced functionality.
days.explanation: Data Structures in Java are like specialized containers for different needs. Think of them as different types of storage furniture: Arrays are like fixed shelves, ArrayLists are like expandable shelves, HashSets are like labeled boxes where each item is unique, and HashMaps are like filing cabinets with labeled folders. Each has its purpose: some keep order, some don't allow duplicates, some allow fast searching. The java.util package provides these ready-to-use structures so you don't have to build them from scratch.
days.real_world_example: Data structures are used everywhere: E-commerce sites use ArrayLists for shopping carts, social media uses HashSets to track unique likes, databases use HashMaps for fast lookups, operating systems use Queues for process scheduling, and compilers use Stacks for syntax checking. When you add items to Amazon cart (ArrayList), when Facebook shows unique friends (HashSet), when your phone stores contacts with names and numbers (HashMap) - all use data structures.
interactive_tasks: Create a phonebook using HashMap with name-phone number pairs
Implement a todo list using ArrayList with add, remove, and mark complete functions
Create a program to find duplicate words in a text using HashSet

quiz.question: Which data structure allows duplicate elements?
quiz.reasoning: ArrayList allows duplicates, while HashSet and TreeSet do not.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
options: ArrayList is faster for random access
LinkedList is faster for random access
quiz.answer: ArrayList is faster for random access
quiz.reasoning: ArrayList provides O(1) random access, while LinkedList requires traversal.

quiz.question: Which data structure stores key-value pairs?
quiz.reasoning: HashMap stores data as key-value pairs for fast lookup by key.

quiz.question: What happens if you add duplicate to HashSet?
quiz.reasoning: HashSet doesn't allow duplicates; attempts to add duplicates are ignored.

quiz.question: Which maintains insertion order?
quiz.reasoning: ArrayList maintains insertion order, while HashSet/HashMap don't guarantee order.

quiz.question: What is LIFO principle associated with?
quiz.reasoning: Stack follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle.

quiz.question: Which is faster for searching: HashMap or TreeMap?
quiz.reasoning: HashMap provides O(1) average search time, while TreeMap provides O(log n).

days.title: Day 31 – Java Collections Framework
days.definition: The Java Collections Framework is a unified architecture in java.util package that provides interfaces (List, Set, Map) and their implementations (ArrayList, HashSet, HashMap, etc.) for storing and manipulating groups of data.
days.explanation: The Collections Framework is like a well-organized toolkit for data handling. Think of interfaces as blueprints (List says 'must have add, remove, get methods') and classes as actual tools (ArrayList is one tool following List blueprint). It's a hierarchy where interfaces define what can be done, and classes provide how to do it. This framework eliminates the need to create data structures from scratch and ensures consistency across Java programs.
days.real_world_example: The Collections Framework is used in every Java application: Spring Framework uses Lists for dependency injection, Hibernate uses Sets for relationships, banking systems use Maps for account lookups, e-commerce sites use ArrayLists for shopping carts, and social media uses HashSets for tracking unique likes. When you see a friend list (LinkedHashSet maintains order), when you search products (HashMap for fast lookup), when you sort items (TreeSet for sorting) - all use Collections Framework.
interactive_tasks: Create a library system with Book objects stored in different collections
Implement a voting system using HashMap to count votes
Create a program that removes duplicates from a list using Set

quiz.question: What is the root interface of Collections Framework?
quiz.reasoning: Collection is the root interface for List and Set hierarchies.

quiz.question: Which maintains insertion order?
quiz.reasoning: LinkedHashSet maintains the order in which elements were inserted.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of using interface references?
quiz.reasoning: Using interfaces allows switching implementations easily.

quiz.question: Which collection provides fastest lookup by key?
quiz.reasoning: HashMap provides O(1) average time for get/put operations.

quiz.question: What does Collections.sort() require?
quiz.reasoning: sort() requires elements to implement Comparable interface.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a List implementation?
quiz.reasoning: TreeList is not part of standard Java Collections Framework.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between Iterator and ListIterator?
quiz.reasoning: ListIterator can traverse in both directions, Iterator only forward.

days.title: Day 32 – Java List Interface
days.definition: The List interface represents an ordered collection that allows duplicate elements and provides indexed access to elements.
days.explanation: List is like a numbered shopping list where items have positions and you can add the same item multiple times. It maintains the order in which you add items and lets you access them by their position number.
days.real_world_example: Used for shopping carts, to-do lists, playlists - anywhere order matters.
interactive_tasks: Create a list of 5 student names
Remove the second student from list
Check if a name exists in list

quiz.question: List allows duplicates?
quiz.reasoning: List interface allows duplicate elements.

quiz.question: How to get element at index 2?
quiz.reasoning: get(index) method retrieves element at specified position.

quiz.question: Which maintains insertion order?
quiz.reasoning: List maintains the order in which elements were added.

days.title: Day 33 – Java ArrayList vs LinkedList
days.definition: ArrayList and LinkedList both implement the List interface but differ in their internal structure: ArrayList uses dynamic array while LinkedList uses doubly-linked list.
days.explanation: ArrayList is like a dynamic bookshelf that expands when full. LinkedList is like a train where each carriage connects to the next. ArrayList is faster for reading, LinkedList is faster for adding/removing in middle.
days.real_world_example: ArrayList: Student list (need fast access by roll number). LinkedList: Browser history (frequent add/remove).
interactive_tasks: Create ArrayList of 5 numbers and get third element
Create LinkedList and add elements at beginning and end
Compare performance for adding in middle

quiz.question: Which is faster for random access?
quiz.reasoning: ArrayList provides O(1) access by index.

quiz.question: Which uses nodes with links?
quiz.reasoning: LinkedList uses nodes connected to next/previous nodes.

quiz.question: addFirst() is available in?
quiz.reasoning: addFirst() is specific to LinkedList class.

days.title: Day 34 – Java List Sorting
days.definition: List sorting in Java organizes elements in a specific order (ascending/descending) using the Collections.sort() method.
days.explanation: Sorting arranges data in a meaningful order, like arranging names alphabetically or numbers from smallest to largest. Java provides easy sorting through Collections class methods.
days.real_world_example: Sorting student names alphabetically, arranging products by price, ordering tasks by priority.
interactive_tasks: Sort list of 5 names alphabetically
Sort list of numbers in descending order
Create and sort list of custom objects

quiz.question: Which class provides sort() method?
quiz.reasoning: Collections.sort() is used to sort List collections.

quiz.question: How to sort in reverse order?
quiz.reasoning: Pass Collections.reverseOrder() as second parameter.

quiz.question: Can we sort custom objects?
quiz.reasoning: Objects must implement Comparable interface.

days.title: Day 35 – Java Set Interface
days.definition: The Set interface stores unique elements and does not allow duplicates, with different implementations for ordering needs.
days.explanation: Set is like a unique club membership - no duplicate members allowed. HashSet doesn't care about order, TreeSet sorts automatically, LinkedHashSet remembers insertion order.
days.real_world_example: Used for storing unique user IDs, removing duplicate email addresses, tracking unique visitors.
interactive_tasks: Create HashSet of 5 colors
Remove duplicates from a list using Set
Find common elements between two sets

quiz.question: Set allows duplicates?
quiz.reasoning: Set interface does not allow duplicate elements.

quiz.question: Which Set maintains sorted order?
quiz.reasoning: TreeSet sorts elements in natural order.

quiz.question: Which operation finds common elements?
quiz.reasoning: Intersection returns elements present in both sets.

days.title: Day 36 – Java HashSet
days.definition: HashSet is an implementation of Set interface that stores unique elements using hash table, providing fast operations but no ordering guarantee.
days.explanation: HashSet is like a bag of unique marbles - you can quickly check if a marble exists, but they're in random order. It uses hashing to store elements, making add, remove, and contains operations very fast.
days.real_world_example: Used for checking unique usernames, finding duplicate files, tracking visited URLs in web crawlers, storing unique product IDs.
interactive_tasks: Create HashSet of 5 student IDs
Check if a specific ID exists
Remove duplicates from array using HashSet

quiz.question: HashSet allows duplicates?
quiz.reasoning: HashSet stores only unique elements.

quiz.question: What is time complexity of contains()?
quiz.reasoning: HashSet provides constant time for contains() on average.

quiz.question: How to create empty HashSet?
quiz.reasoning: All are valid ways to create HashSet.

days.title: Day 37 – Java TreeSet
days.definition: TreeSet is a Set implementation that stores unique elements in sorted order using a Red-Black tree structure.
days.explanation: TreeSet is like a sorted bookshelf that automatically arranges books alphabetically. It maintains elements in natural order (ascending) and provides efficient operations for sorted collections.
days.real_world_example: Used for maintaining sorted student grades, storing unique words in dictionary order, keeping leaderboard scores sorted, storing dates in chronological order.
interactive_tasks: Create TreeSet of 5 names and display sorted
Find elements greater than given value
Create TreeSet sorted by custom criteria

quiz.question: TreeSet maintains elements in?
quiz.reasoning: TreeSet stores elements in natural sorted order.

quiz.question: What is time complexity of add()?
quiz.reasoning: TreeSet uses Red-Black tree with O(log n) operations.

quiz.question: Which method gets smallest element?
quiz.reasoning: first() returns the lowest element in TreeSet.

days.title: Day 38 – Java LinkedHashSet
days.definition: LinkedHashSet is a Set implementation that combines HashSet's uniqueness with LinkedList's insertion order preservation.
days.explanation: LinkedHashSet is like a queue of unique people - no duplicates allowed, and people stay in the order they joined. It maintains a doubly-linked list across all entries to remember insertion order.
days.real_world_example: Used for browser history (unique sites in visit order), shopping cart items, maintaining insertion order in caches, tracking unique user actions in sequence.
interactive_tasks: Create LinkedHashSet of 5 colors in specific order
Remove middle element and verify order
Create LRU cache with size limit

quiz.question: LinkedHashSet maintains?
quiz.reasoning: LinkedHashSet preserves the order elements were added.

quiz.question: Which is faster?
quiz.reasoning: HashSet is fastest as it doesn't maintain order.

quiz.question: LinkedHashSet allows duplicates?
quiz.reasoning: Like all Sets, LinkedHashSet doesn't allow duplicates.

days.title: Day 39 – Java Map Interface
days.definition: The Map interface stores key-value pairs where each key is unique, allowing fast lookup by key.
days.explanation: Map is like a dictionary - each word (key) has a definition (value). Keys must be unique, but values can repeat. It provides efficient lookup, insertion, and deletion of pairs.
days.real_world_example: Used for phone books (name->number), user databases (ID->user), configuration settings (key->value), word counters (word->count).
interactive_tasks: Create Map of 3 country-capital pairs
Find value for specific key
Iterate and print all key-value pairs

quiz.question: Map keys must be?
quiz.reasoning: Each key in a Map must be unique.

quiz.question: Which method gets value by key?
quiz.reasoning: get(key) returns the value associated with the key.

quiz.question: How to get all keys?
quiz.reasoning: keySet() returns a Set containing all keys.

days.title: Day 40 – Java HashMap
days.definition: HashMap is a Map implementation that stores key-value pairs using hash table, providing fast access but no ordering guarantee.
days.explanation: HashMap is like a smart dictionary - you give it a word (key) and instantly get the definition (value). It uses hashing to store data, making operations very fast on average.
days.real_world_example: Used for caching (URL->page), user sessions (sessionID->user), database indexing (ID->record), configuration settings.
interactive_tasks: Create HashMap of 3 products with prices
Find price for specific product
Count word frequencies in sentence

quiz.question: HashMap allows null key?
quiz.reasoning: HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values.

quiz.question: What is time complexity of get()?
quiz.reasoning: HashMap provides constant time for get() on average.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a way to iterate?
quiz.reasoning: values() returns Collection, not valueSet().

days.title: Day 41 – Streams, Collectors & Functional Pipelines
days.definition: Streams process sequences of data declaratively with map/filter/reduce pipelines, avoiding boilerplate loops.

explanation.main: Streams let you describe data transformations as a pipeline of operations rather than nested loops.
key_points: Use collect() with Collectors to build lists, maps, or summaries
Short-circuit operations (findFirst, anyMatch) reduce work when possible
ParallelStream can leverage multi-core CPUs when tasks are independent

days.real_world_example: Back-end services convert request payloads into DTOs using stream pipelines before persisting to databases.
interactive_tasks: Filter and sort a list of users by age with streams
Group orders by status using Collectors.groupingBy
Create a stream that stops early with findFirst

quiz.question: What does Collectors.toList() do?
options: Collects stream results into a List
quiz.answer: Collects stream results into a List
quiz.reasoning: Collectors.toList() accumulates stream items into a List.

quiz.question: Which operation short-circuits?
quiz.reasoning: anyMatch may stop once a matching element is found.

quiz.question: How do you run stream operations in parallel?
quiz.reasoning: parallelStream() or stream().parallel() both create parallel streams.

learning_objectives: Build pipelines with streams and collectors
Read data declaratively instead of loops

sections.heading: Pipeline Tips
content: Keep operations stateless for parallel streams
Use peek() only for debugging when necessary
Avoid side effects in mapping functions

tips: Avoid parallel streams when operations hit external services

days.title: Day 42 – CompletableFuture & Structured Concurrency
days.definition: CompletableFuture composes asynchronous tasks, while structured concurrency keeps cancellation and propagation predictable.

explanation.main: Chain futures to describe the flow of asynchronous tasks and handle errors in one place.
key_points: SupplyAsync submits tasks to an ExecutorService
Use CompletableFuture.allOf to wait on multiple tasks

days.real_world_example: HTTP gateways launch multiple service calls with CompletableFuture and compose responses before replying to the client.
interactive_tasks: Combine two asynchronous API calls using thenCombine
Handle timeout by adding orTimeout() to a future
Create an ExecutorService for CPU-bound tasks and pass it to supplyAsync

quiz.question: Which method creates a future that is already completed?
quiz.reasoning: CompletableFuture.completedFuture(value) returns an already completed future.

quiz.question: What does thenCompose do?
quiz.reasoning: thenCompose chains futures without nesting CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>.

quiz.question: How do you handle exceptions in a chain?
quiz.reasoning: exceptionally lets you return a fallback when an exception occurs.

learning_objectives: Use structured concurrency helpers like allOf

sections.heading: Concurrency Checklist
content: Provide a dedicated ExecutorService when CPU-bound
Avoid blocking inside supplyAsync to keep threads available

tips: Call join() only after all compose steps complete

days.title: Day 43 – Architectures, Patterns & Reactive Thinking
days.definition: Combine design patterns, modules, and reactive principles to build maintainable server-side systems.

explanation.main: Apply strategy and builder patterns, divide code with modules, and design services that react to events.
key_points: Strategy & Template Method simplify swapping behavior
Modules expose only required interfaces with module-info.java
Reactive streams (Flux, Flow) help manage backpressure
Use dependency injection to decouple layers

days.real_world_example: Microservices use dependency injection frameworks with strategy patterns to swap database drivers per environment.
interactive_tasks: Write two CompressionStrategy implementations and swap them via configuration
Add module-info.java that opens packages to reflection for frameworks
Simulate reactive backpressure with Flow.Publisher and Flow.Subscriber

quiz.question: What problem does the Strategy pattern solve?
quiz.reasoning: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable behaviors.

quiz.question: Which file defines modules in Java 9+?
quiz.reasoning: module-info.java declares module exports, requires, and opens.

quiz.question: Reactive streams help with ____?
quiz.reasoning: Reactive streams coordinate producers and consumers to avoid overwhelming subscribers.

learning_objectives: Apply behavioral design patterns for flexible components
Use module boundaries for cleaner encapsulation
Think reactively about event, stream, and I/O flows

sections.heading: Architectural Focus
content: Use dependency injection to swap implementations
Define module exits and dependencies explicitly
Protect modules with clear API surfaces

tips: Document module exports to clarify public APIs
Test strategy swaps with different configurations
